There is no controversy regard ISR.  People had them but less 1% discontinued in the clinical trial due to ISR.   
 
Yes, the data from Nektar’s own Phase 2b trials (REZOLVE-AD in atopic dermatitis and REZOLVE-AA in alopecia areata) support what you heard: injection site reactions (ISRs) are common but almost never lead to patients stopping treatment.  
 
ir.nektar.com 
 
In the 16-week induction period of REZOLVE-AD:ISRs occurred in about 70% of rezpeg-treated patients (vs ~4% on placebo). 
99.6% were mild or moderate. 
Discontinuations due to ISR were under 1% (specifically reported as 0.6%). 
Most were self-resolving.  
 
ir.nektar.com 
 
Later 52-week data showed a similar picture: discontinuation due to ISR around 0.7%, with ISRs becoming less frequent during maintenance dosing (every 4 or 12 weeks). In the alopecia trial, Nektar reported zero discontinuations due to ISR.  
 
ir.nektar.com 
 
In short: high incidence of (mostly mild) ISRs is real and has been a talking point, especially from Lilly and some analysts. But the claim that patients are frequently stopping treatment because of them is not supported by the Phase 2b data Nektar has presented. The disagreement is more about how commercially relevant the reactions will be than about the discontinuation numbers themselves.
